section_summary: This section begins with Chinese and British criticism of Great Britain’s short-lived 1933 arms embargo and Department of State deliberations over collective sanctions against Japan, China, and Peru. It then records a series of 1934–1935 inquiries concerning American exports to Japan, including firearms, aircraft, engines, manufacturing licenses, technical data, explosives, and helium. Much of the later correspondence concerns interdepartmental review of military secrets and the conditions under which civilian or previously released technology could be transferred to Japanese companies.

subfiles.title: “The British Arms Embargo” editorial from China Times
subfiles.about: A Chinese editorial condemns Britain’s nondiscriminatory arms embargo on both China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial argues that equal restrictions on China and Japan weaken the defending state while benefiting the aggressor. It also accuses Great Britain of contradicting Sir John Simon’s insistence that an embargo could work only through international action.

subfiles.title: “British Quixotry: The Arms Embargo”
subfiles.about: Woodhead criticizes Britain’s arms embargo as ineffective, unfair to China, and damaging to British aircraft manufacturers.
subfiles.summary: The column argues that China depends more heavily than Japan on imported arms and therefore bears the greater burden of an ostensibly neutral embargo. It predicts that buyers will turn to American, French, or German aircraft and characterizes the policy as a futile moral gesture and a commercial blunder.

subfiles.title: Division of Regional Information routing slip
subfiles.about: An internal slip records action taken in accordance with a telephone request.
subfiles.summary: The surviving text states that material was furnished in response to a telephone request. It appears to serve as a transmittal for the Commerce Department export statistics that follow.

subfiles.title: United States Exports of Firearms, Explosives, Aircraft, and Parts to Japan, 1931–1932
subfiles.about: The statement tabulates American exports of weapons, ammunition, explosives, aircraft, engines, and aircraft parts to Japan in 1931 and 1932.
subfiles.summary: The tables enumerate quantities and values for firearms, ammunition, explosives, aircraft, engines, and accessories shipped to Japan. A note records that the original statement was sent, without a covering letter, to Ching-Lin Hsia of the Chinese Legation.

subfiles.title: Memorandum concerning Military Attaché report on the British embargo
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes an attached Military Attaché report quoting British opposition to the arms embargo.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum highlights an editorial in The Army, Navy and Air Force Gazette arguing that Britain should avoid the Far Eastern dispute. It quotes the view that China and Japan would obtain arms elsewhere if Britain refused to supply them.

subfiles.title: Report No. 3550, “Criticism of British Far Eastern Policy”
subfiles.about: The report reproduces a British military journal editorial opposing the embargo on arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The editorial warns that the embargo could encourage anti-European agitation in China without stopping supplies of oil, cotton, nitrates, or indirectly re-exported weapons. It argues that Britain should avoid the dispute, doubts Soviet compliance, and stresses the harm to British armament industries and employment.
keywords: The Army, Navy and Air Force Gazette

subfiles.title: Memorandum transmitting Gilbert Murray’s arms-embargo message
subfiles.about: The memorandum records Professor Shotwell’s telephone transmission of a telegram from Professor Gilbert Murray.
subfiles.summary: Shotwell told the Department that he had just received Murray’s statement on an arms embargo. The memorandum introduces the telephone transcription filed on the following page.

subfiles.title: League of Nations Union resolution on discriminatory sanctions
subfiles.from: Gilbert Murray, relayed by James T. Shotwell
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.about: The message urges international, discriminatory action against a state found guilty of aggression.
subfiles.summary: The Executive League of Nations Union welcomes the principle that peace obligations should take precedence over trade. It calls the temporary embargo on both China and Japan an interim measure and urges League, American, and Russian cooperation in withholding arms and financial assistance from the aggressor.

subfiles.title: Docket abstract of H. A. James Jr.’s motor-patent letter
subfiles.about: The abstract describes an inventor’s remorse over negotiations to sell a patented motor to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The docket states that the writer was negotiating with the Japanese Government over a patented motor. It notes that he wrote the President because he regretted selling the patent rights to a foreign power.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning sale of a patented motor to Japan
subfiles.about: James reports negotiations to sell the Japanese Government rights to a fuel-saving motor and expresses misgivings about the transaction.
subfiles.summary: James claims that his motor would reduce gasoline consumption substantially and says concern for the public interest has troubled his conscience. He explains that he intended to sell rights only for Japan, but the Japanese representative sought rights for the entire world.

subfiles.title: Reply to H. A. James Jr.
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the White House referral of James’s letter about selling his motor to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton confirms receipt, through the White House, of James’s April 20 letter. The reply merely identifies the subject and offers no substantive ruling on the proposed sale.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on H.J. Resolution 93
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to a memorandum supporting an arms-embargo resolution before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
subfiles.summary: It identifies a memorandum read by Green during an executive session of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations. The referenced document discussed how H.J. Resolution 93 would operate in conflicts between China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Personal letter on embargo policy after the Geneva meetings
subfiles.about: Wilson assesses the international politics, responsibilities, and risks of arms embargoes in the Manchurian and Leticia disputes.
subfiles.summary: Wilson reports that arms-producing states are awaiting an American lead and that European states view the disputes as precedents for an automatic system against aggressors. He contrasts consultation with Britain, France, and Italy with an independent American refusal to embargo Japan alone. He warns that moving from nonrecognition to active sanctions could provoke Japanese retaliation and expand from arms restrictions to raw-material embargoes and complete economic severance.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 159 from Geneva on arms-producing states
subfiles.about: Wilson reports that other arms-producing countries are likely to make their embargo policies contingent on the United States.
subfiles.summary: Wilson believes that an American decision for or against an embargo on Peru would determine the positions taken by other producing states. He finds policy toward Japan less certain because of British reservations, although France might support a Japan-only embargo. He recommends prior consultation with Britain, France, and Italy and warns that other powers are attempting to shift responsibility onto the United States.

subfiles.title: Hull’s reply to Hugh R. Wilson
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Wilson’s March 29 letter and refers to instructions embodying the administration’s chosen embargo policy.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Wilson for his views on the complicated arms-embargo question. He expresses the hope that subsequent instructions have stated the adopted policy with sufficient precision.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Sir Robert Vansittart on the British arms embargo
subfiles.about: Hornbeck and Vansittart discuss why Britain imposed and then lifted its embargo on arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Vansittart says the embargo was imposed hastily because some ministers felt something had to be done, without adequate study of treaty implications or practical effects. He states that the policy was abandoned when it proved unworkable and that Japan had apparently made no treaty-based protest. The conversation then turns to Japanese military intentions in North China, British inquiries at Tokyo, and reports that operations would stop at the Luan River.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to D. F. Giera inquiry on explosives exports
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a letter asking about the laws governing exports of explosives to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The entry identifies D. F. Giera’s inquiry concerning explosives shipments to Japan. The substantive letter was filed under decimal number 811.115/342 rather than in this file.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to William Floyd arms-sales inquiry
subfiles.about: The sheet points to correspondence asking whether American manufacturers could sell arms to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: William Floyd sought clarification on whether an embargo barred American arms sales to either belligerent. The underlying War Department letter was filed as 811.113/343.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation on shipment of a Cyclone airplane engine
subfiles.about: A Wright Aeronautical representative asks whether shipment of a Cyclone engine and plans to Mitsui in Japan requires a State Department license.
subfiles.summary: Vaughan states that the War and Navy Departments have approved the proposed shipment. Mackay replies that the State Department requires no export license for the engine but advises the company to ensure full compliance with War and Navy Department requirements.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy request concerning a Consolidated P2Y2 flying boat
subfiles.about: The Japanese Ambassador requests assistance in securing permission for Mitsui to purchase a Consolidated Model P2Y2 flying boat.
subfiles.summary: Mitsui was negotiating with Consolidated Aircraft Corporation for the aircraft. The note states that the Japanese side understood that the manufacturer had already applied to the United States Government for export permission.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the P2Y2 export inquiry
subfiles.about: Green records the result of Lieutenant Lawton’s investigation of the proposed P2Y2 export.
subfiles.summary: Lawton reports that Consolidated Aircraft had not applied for export permission. Because the P2Y2 was the latest model and incorporated military secrets, the responsible authorities would not authorize its export.

subfiles.title: Reply denying export of the P2Y2 flying boat
subfiles.about: The Department informs the Japanese Embassy that the P2Y2 flying boat cannot be exported because it contains military secrets.
subfiles.summary: The reply notes that Consolidated Aircraft had not submitted the asserted export application. It states that permission could not then be granted because the model embodied protected military features.

subfiles.title: Japanese acknowledgment of the P2Y2 decision
subfiles.about: The Ambassador acknowledges the American refusal to permit Mitsui to purchase a P2Y2 flying boat.
subfiles.summary: The note thanks the Secretary for his May 24 response. It repeats that the model could not be sold because it embodied military secrets.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to April 1934 arms-export statistics
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Department of State
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies a Commerce Department list of American arms and ammunition exports to Japan during April 1934.
subfiles.summary: The referenced list covered arms, ammunition, and implements of war exported from the United States to Japan. The substantive statement was filed under decimal number 824.113/119.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Du Pont sales to Japan
subfiles.from: E. I. du Pont de Nemours & Company
subfiles.about: The sheet points to correspondence about Du Pont’s sale of a hydrogen process and munitions of war to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The record concerns potential Du Pont transfers to Japan involving both industrial technology and munitions. The underlying letter was placed in another decimal-file series.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on Du Pont machinery and explosives
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Department of State
subfiles.about: The sheet points to Green’s discussion with a Du Pont director about sales of machinery and explosives to the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: The referenced memorandum recorded a discussion between Green and Mr. Casey of Du Pont. It stated that D. F. Giera was conducting negotiations as agent for the Japanese Military Mission.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on D. F. Giera’s commission scheme
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Department of State
subfiles.about: The sheet summarizes suspicions that an explosives transaction was intended to conceal commissions on Japanese purchases.
subfiles.summary: Green believed Giera’s proposed explosives sale was a device to disguise commissions. The alleged beneficiaries were Giera and the Japanese Military Mission in connection with purchases made in the United States.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to the War Department about German arms shipments
subfiles.from: William Phillips for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: George H. Dern, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: The State Department requests more information about five German ships reported to be carrying arms through Manila to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Phillips cites an August Philippine Department intelligence digest reporting the transit of five German vessels with arms and munitions. He asks whether the cargo originated in German factories or in factories located in countries bordering Germany.

subfiles.title: War Department reply on German vessels bound for Yokohama
subfiles.from: George H. Dern, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: The War Department supplies the limited information available about German ships carrying possible arms cargoes through Manila.
subfiles.summary: A quoted radiogram says Manila authorities kept no manifest for cargo merely passing through the port. It lists the vessels’ ports of origin as Genoa, Bremen, and Hamburg and their terminal destination as Yokohama, but reports that no further information could be obtained.

subfiles.title: Auto-Ordnance inquiry on Thompson submachine guns for Mitsui
subfiles.from: W. B. Ryan Jr., Auto-Ordnance Corporation
subfiles.about: Auto-Ordnance asks whether the Department objects to quoting prices to Mitsui for Thompson submachine guns.
subfiles.summary: Ryan encloses Mitsui’s December 18 inquiry and explains that the company routinely seeks State Department guidance before quoting foreign buyers. Auto-Ordnance is withholding its reply to Mitsui pending the Department’s opinion.

subfiles.title: Mitsui request for submachine-gun quotation
subfiles.about: Mitsui requests prices for one or two submachine guns and ammunition for Nakajima Aircraft Company pilots.
subfiles.summary: Mitsui says Nakajima wants the weapons for pilots’ self-defense during aircraft testing in the desert. It requests a quotation for police-type submachine guns and one thousand rounds of service ammunition per gun.

subfiles.title: Reply on export of Thompson submachine guns
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department advises that no treaty or statute generally prohibits exporting Thompson submachine guns to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton states that the proposed articles are not barred from export to Japan. He nevertheless directs Auto-Ordnance to the National Firearms Act of June 28, 1934, particularly its procedural requirements for exporting machine guns.

subfiles.title: Navy Department transmittal on Curtiss Hawk landing-gear license
subfiles.from: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The Navy forwards and conditionally endorses a proposed Curtiss manufacturing license for Mitsubishi.
subfiles.summary: The War and Navy Departments find no military-secrecy objection to licensing the previously released Curtiss Hawk retractable landing gear. They require deletion of the clause granting Mitsubishi first refusal on future improvements and exclude later modifications from the authorization.

subfiles.title: Curtiss request for approval of Mitsubishi landing-gear license
subfiles.from: Robert L. Earle, Curtiss Aeroplane & Motor Company
subfiles.to: Chief, Bureau of Aeronautics, Navy Department
subfiles.about: Curtiss seeks approval to sell Mitsubishi a retractable landing gear, manufacturing rights, and associated technical data.
subfiles.summary: Earle explains that the gear had already been released for foreign sale and that negotiations with Mitsubishi were complete. He also requests permission for Mitsubishi engineers to inspect the gear and receive blueprints while being isolated from sensitive work elsewhere in the Buffalo plant.

subfiles.title: Mitsubishi Order TR-5911 for Curtiss retractable landing gear
subfiles.about: Mitsubishi orders a Curtiss Hawk retractable landing gear and an exclusive Japanese manufacturing license.
subfiles.summary: The order covers a complete landing-gear set, design analysis, drawings, specifications, and die-making data for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. Its special terms grant exclusivity in Japan and its possessions, access for Mitsubishi engineers at Buffalo, and a first-refusal right on later improvements. The last provision became the principal objection raised by the War and Navy Departments.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal to the Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Phillips acknowledges the Navy’s advice and encloses the State Department’s response to Curtiss concerning the landing-gear license.
subfiles.summary: The letter identifies the proposed transfer of Curtiss Hawk landing-gear manufacturing rights to Mitsubishi. It sends the Navy a copy of the conditional approval communicated to Curtiss.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal to the Secretary of War
subfiles.to: George H. Dern, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Phillips sends the War Department a copy of the reply to Curtiss on the proposed Mitsubishi license.
subfiles.summary: The letter concerns Curtiss’s plan to grant Mitsubishi rights to manufacture the Hawk retractable landing gear. It provides the Secretary of War with the Department’s formal response for his information.

subfiles.title: Conditional approval of Curtiss landing-gear license
subfiles.from: Pierrepont Moffat for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Robert L. Earle, Curtiss Aeroplane & Motor Company
subfiles.about: The Department approves the Mitsubishi landing-gear license subject to restrictions imposed by the War and Navy Departments.
subfiles.summary: Moffat states that the defense departments have no secrecy objection to the agreement for the previously released Curtiss Hawk gear. Approval requires deletion of special-term paragraph three and excludes all future modifications or improvements from the release.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to January 1935 arms-export statement
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies a statement of American arms and ammunition exports to Japan during January 1935.
subfiles.summary: The referenced Commerce Department document listed arms, ammunition, and implements of war exported from the United States to Japan. It was filed under decimal number 824.113/420.

subfiles.title: Lockheed inquiry on Electra manufacturing rights
subfiles.from: Robert E. Gross, Lockheed Aircraft Corporation
subfiles.about: Lockheed asks whether the Department would object to selling Japanese interests the manufacturing rights and technical data for its Electra transport.
subfiles.summary: Gross describes the Electra as an entirely commercial but advanced design and anticipates an approach from interests close to the Japanese Government. Lockheed believes there should be no objection but seeks confirmation before entering negotiations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum confirming civilian status of the Electra
subfiles.about: Green records military confirmation that the Lockheed Electra involves no protected secret.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Burnett of the Military Intelligence Division confirms by telephone that the Electra is a civilian transport. He states that it contains no military secret.

subfiles.title: Reply approving sale of Electra manufacturing rights
subfiles.from: Pierrepont Moffat for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department states that no legal or military-secrecy restriction bars sale of Electra manufacturing rights to Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: Moffat explains that only restrictions administered by the Secretaries of War and Navy could affect the proposed transfer. The War Department has advised that the Electra transport contains no military secrets.

subfiles.title: Electra correspondence transmitted to the Navy Department
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Phillips sends the Navy copies of Lockheed’s Electra inquiry and the State Department’s reply.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure concerns possible Japanese purchase of the Electra’s manufacturing rights, designs, and engineering data. The Navy receives both Lockheed’s request and the Department’s favorable response for information.

subfiles.title: Electra correspondence transmitted to the War Department
subfiles.to: George H. Dern, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Phillips sends the War Department copies of Lockheed’s inquiry and the reply permitting an Electra technology transfer.
subfiles.summary: The letter identifies the possible Japanese purchase of Electra manufacturing rights and engineering data. It provides the War Department with the company’s request and State’s response.

subfiles.title: War Department conditions for Pratt & Whitney–Mitsubishi engine license
subfiles.from: George H. Dern, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: The War Department forwards a Pratt & Whitney engine-license request and lists conditions for its approval.
subfiles.summary: War and Navy raise no secrecy objection to Mitsubishi’s licensed manufacture of specified Hornet engines. The conditions preserve the Government’s right to withdraw export approval, disclaim wartime sales rights, restrict Mitsubishi technicians to nonsensitive plant areas, and oppose visits by Pratt & Whitney personnel to assist production in Japan.

subfiles.title: Pratt & Whitney request for approval of Mitsubishi agreement
subfiles.from: H. M. Horner, Pratt & Whitney Aircraft Company
subfiles.about: Pratt & Whitney seeks approval of its license agreement with Mitsubishi for Hornet aircraft engines.
subfiles.summary: Horner says the agreement follows the essential terms of previously approved foreign licenses and adequately protects United States interests. Pricing was removed from the submitted copies as irrelevant to the Government’s review.

subfiles.title: State Department response to the Secretary of War on the Hornet license
subfiles.to: George H. Dern, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Phillips acknowledges the War Department’s review and sends a copy of State’s response to Pratt & Whitney.
subfiles.summary: The letter concerns the recently executed Mitsubishi manufacturing license for Pratt & Whitney engines. It transmits the formal conditional approval sent to the company.

subfiles.title: Hornet-license response transmitted to the Navy Department
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Phillips sends the Navy a copy of the State Department’s response concerning Pratt & Whitney’s Mitsubishi agreement.
subfiles.summary: The correspondence concerns licensed Japanese manufacture of Pratt & Whitney aircraft engines. The Navy is furnished the company reply for its information.

subfiles.title: Conditional approval of Pratt & Whitney–Mitsubishi engine agreement
subfiles.from: Pierrepont Moffat for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department conditionally approves Mitsubishi’s licensed manufacture of Pratt & Whitney Hornet engines.
subfiles.summary: The approval preserves the Government’s authority to revoke consent and grants no right to ship or sell licensed engines in the territory during wartime. Mitsubishi representatives must remain outside plant areas containing government work, and the Government discourages Pratt & Whitney personnel from traveling to Japan to assist production.

subfiles.title: Navy acknowledgment of the Pratt & Whitney reply
subfiles.about: The Navy acknowledges receipt of State’s letter and its enclosure concerning the Mitsubishi engine license.
subfiles.summary: The letter confirms receipt of the State Department’s April 23 communication. It specifically identifies the enclosed reply to Pratt & Whitney about its manufacturing-license agreement with Mitsubishi.

subfiles.title: Pratt & Whitney acknowledgment of license restrictions
subfiles.from: D. L. Brown, Pratt & Whitney Aircraft Company
subfiles.about: Pratt & Whitney acknowledges the Department’s conditions on its Mitsubishi manufacturing license.
subfiles.summary: Brown confirms receipt of Moffat’s April 23 letter. He states that the company will follow the restrictions governing Mitsubishi technicians and visits by Pratt & Whitney personnel to Japan.

subfiles.title: Navy acknowledgment of Electra correspondence
subfiles.from: W. H. Standley, Acting Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The Navy acknowledges State’s correspondence about possible Japanese purchase of Lockheed Electra manufacturing rights.
subfiles.summary: Standley confirms receipt of Lockheed’s letter and the State Department’s response. The materials concern manufacturing rights, designs, and engineering data for the Electra transport airplane.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Fairchild radio-compass inquiry
subfiles.about: The sheet points to correspondence about selling G. G. Kruesi’s patented radio compass to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The referenced letter concerns Fairchild Aerial Camera Corporation’s interest in Japanese sales of the compass. The substantive document was filed under decimal number 811.113/568.

subfiles.title: Navy transmittal of Eclipse Aviation license request
subfiles.from: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The Navy forwards and recommends approval of Eclipse Aviation’s proposed license to Mitsui for aircraft electrical equipment.
subfiles.summary: The request concerns Japanese manufacture of specified generators, dynamotors, and external energizers. War and Navy conclude that military secrets present no objection and recommend that Eclipse be informed favorably.

subfiles.title: Eclipse Aviation request for Japanese manufacturing license
subfiles.from: R. P. Lansing, Eclipse Aviation Corporation
subfiles.about: Eclipse seeks permission to license Mitsui to manufacture specified aircraft generators, dynamotors, and an energizer in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter lists the models and ratings to be covered and notes that Mitsui already holds a license for certain Eclipse starters. Eclipse proposes limiting the agreement to equipment already released for foreign sale and excluding later improvements, developments, and experimental work unless separately authorized.

subfiles.title: State Department response to the Navy on the Eclipse license
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Welles acknowledges the Navy’s recommendation and encloses State’s reply to Eclipse Aviation.
subfiles.summary: The letter identifies the proposed Mitsui license for specified aircraft electrical equipment in Japan. It sends the Navy a copy of the favorable response issued to Eclipse.

subfiles.title: Eclipse-license response transmitted to the War Department
subfiles.to: George H. Dern, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Secretary of War a copy of its reply approving Eclipse Aviation’s proposed Mitsui license.
subfiles.summary: The proposed agreement covers manufacture in Japan of specified aircraft electrical equipment. The War Department receives the company reply for its information.

subfiles.title: Approval of Eclipse Aviation–Mitsui license agreement
subfiles.from: Pierrepont Moffat for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department advises Eclipse that the War and Navy Departments have no military-secrecy objection to its proposed Mitsui license.
subfiles.summary: Moffat confirms that defense officials approve the agreement for manufacture of the specified equipment in Japan. He adds that no other treaty or statute restricts American companies from licensing foreign manufacture of arms or implements of war, apart from military-secret controls administered by War and Navy.

subfiles.title: Navy Department letter opposing export of helium
subfiles.about: The Navy forwards a Helium Company request and explains its opposition to exporting commercially produced helium.
subfiles.summary: The Navy calls helium a strategic military asset whose American monopoly should be preserved and argues that exports would aid foreign commercial competitors in lighter-than-air transportation. It therefore rejects the proposed export and assumes that Japan would have little interest in the accompanying repurification equipment without access to helium; the letter continues beyond this section.
